items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The Chaco-Santiagueña region of South America has long been regarded as marginal to agricultural development, with subsistence systems usually described as mixed foraging and low-intensity horticulture. Here, we present the first integrated stable isotope analysis (δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C and δ
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    N) of human and faunal bone collagen from the Dry Chaco, spanning the last ~1600 years. This dataset is assessed together with modern plant and animal isotopic baselines and regional radiocarbon summed probability distributions (SPDs). Our results reveal a clear temporal shift in camelid isotopic values. Specimens from the late ceramic period (after ~1000–800 BP) are enriched in both δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C and δ
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    N relative to earlier contexts. Mixing models indicate a greater contribution of C
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    resources, while human samples show very high δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C values consistent with a substantial intake of maize or other C
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    -linked foods. These patterns suggest a sustained reorganization of subsistence practices, rather than merely occasional or small-scale horticulture. Contrary to expectations, the isotopic data do not clearly separate camelids morphometrically assigned to wild (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Lama guanicoe</jats:italic>
                    ) and domestic (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Lama glama</jats:italic>
                    ) forms. Both groups show substantial isotopic overlap and marked dietary heterogeneity. This result highlights the limits of osteometric classification alone and supports the use of isotopic proxies for reconstructing animal management, foraging behavior, and landscape use. Regional SPDs show no significant demographic departures at local scales, although the aggregated dataset suggests episodic population fluctuations broadly consistent with isotopic evidence for increased C
                    <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
                    consumption. Taken together, these results challenge the long-standing characterization of the Chaco-Santiagueña region as a marginal agricultural zone. Instead, they point to a dynamic late Holocene mosaic in which maize cultivation, camelid exploitation or management, and the continued use of wild resources were closely intertwined.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Windblown dunes are found everywhere in the Solar System where a supply of loose sediment is mobilized by gas flows, from the sluggish winds of Venus to speed-of-sound sublimation flows on comets. Their abundance is nontrivial because dunes only form where grains hop ballistically (“saltate”). This implies that winds across the Solar System reach “goldilocks” speeds that are just right to initiate and maintain saltation of whatever sediment is available despite vast variations in material and fluid properties, and gravity. Based on select observations, it was proposed that dune fields may be characterized by a near-threshold transport state where dune-forming winds minimally exceed the saltation threshold on Earth. Here, we demonstrate that this is indeed the case globally. Next, we show that, unlike riverbeds—which evolve to a similar state through adjustments of channel geometry—dune fields are born in it due to the rapid decrease in wind frequency with increasing wind speed. These results imply that grain sizes in windblown dunes provide a robust record of formative winds, such that corresponding wind speeds can be estimated from aeolian sandstones and dune deposits across planets. The near-threshold state of windblown dunes thus opens a promising line of investigation for paleoenvironmental and paleoclimate reconstructions on Earth and beyond.</jats:p>

items.title: Windblown dunes are born in sand at the brink of transport

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The
                    <jats:italic>Tachysurus argentivittatus</jats:italic>
                    group represents the smallest‐bodied lineage within
                    <jats:italic>Tachysurus</jats:italic>
                    with adults not exceeding 50 mm in standard length (SL), and is widely distributed across East Asia. Owing to pronounced morphological conservatism, species delimitation within this group has long been challenging. Previous studies recognized two species within this species group,
                    <jats:italic>T. argentivittatus</jats:italic>
                    sensu stricto, restricted to the Pearl River and
                    <jats:italic>Tachysurus mica</jats:italic>
                    , distributed from the Yangtze to the Amur Rivers and also indicated that the Hainan Island population represents an undescribed lineage. In this study, geographic sampling encompasses the northern margin of the East Asian tropics, including populations from central and northern Vietnam and coastal mainland China. Using an integrative framework, we confirm the validity of
                    <jats:italic>Tachysurus longispinalis</jats:italic>
                    from the Red River basin. Furthermore, this species forms part of a species complex, comprising four reciprocally monophyletic lineages. Within this complex, two allopatric lineages from Hainan Island and the Moyang River (in Guangdong Province of China) exhibit consistent genetic divergence and diagnostic morphological differences, and are described herein as
                    <jats:italic>Tachysurus lativittatus</jats:italic>
                    sp. nov. and
                    <jats:italic>Tachysurus stenomaculatus</jats:italic>
                    sp. nov., respectively. The central Vietnam lineage shows shallow genetic divergence and limited morphological differentiation from
                    <jats:italic>T. longispinalis</jats:italic>
                    and is provisionally treated as
                    <jats:italic>T.</jats:italic>
                    aff.
                    <jats:italic>longispinalis</jats:italic>
                    . Divergence‐time estimates suggest that diversification within the complex occurred from the late Pliocene to the middle Pleistocene, potentially overlapping with major climatic transitions associated with the onset and intensification of Northern Hemisphere glaciation. Repeated sea‐level declines during this period may have facilitated ancestral dispersal and subsequent divergence. Moreover, our findings refine the morphological boundaries of the
                    <jats:italic>T. argentivittatus</jats:italic>
                    group.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract: The evolution of hunter-gatherer subsistence strategies in Mainland Southeast Asia remains poorly understood. While recent studies have explored the hunting behaviors of Late Pleistocene and early Holocene Hoabinhian groups, most research has focused on sedentary populations from the later Holocene. Nevertheless, hunter-gatherer communities persisted into recent times in certain areas, including southern Thailand, and their archaeological record is only beginning to be systematically investigated.Khao Ta Plai (Chumphon Province, southern Thailand), currently excavated by the Fine Arts Department of Thailand, provides new insights into this issue. Archaeological materials uncovered from two excavation pits reveal a long occupational chronology across the Late Pleistocene, Neolithic, and Metal Ages, alongside evidence of geographical diversity in site use. Over 20,000 faunal assemblages provide beneficial data related to prehistoric hunting behaviors. Zooarchaeological and taphonomic investigations suggest continuous exploitation of wild animals throughout all stratigraphic layers. While the relative abundance of specific taxa changes over time, the representation of reptile remains, especially turtles are predominant in several occupation layers.These findings enable us to clarify how hunter-gatherer subsistence strategies emerged alongside innovations in technology, such as ceramics and metallurgy.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Fluvial microvertebrate assemblages are important but underexplored archives for reconstructing Quaternary environments, particularly in regions lacking karstic and cave deposits. We analyse late Middle and early Late Pleistocene small‐vertebrate assemblages from the Middle Dnipro region, Ukraine, to compare two interpretative frameworks: habitat‐weighting analysis and bioclimatic spectra. The studied assemblages span multiple Marine Isotope Stages (MIS 11 to MIS 5) and derive exclusively from alluvial contexts characterised by taphonomic overprinting and time‐averaging. Using principal component analysis, we compare the environmental signals extracted by both methods across different taxonomic datasets. In both approaches, the dominant source of variation reflects changes in ecological evenness, expressed as shifts in the relative importance of steppe, tundra–steppe and high‐latitude taxa. The most even assemblages correspond to cold‐stage conditions and are characterised by arctic and boreal elements, whereas low‐evenness assemblages are dominated by core tundra–steppe taxa. Habitat spectra additionally capture geomorphological influences related to river‐valley dynamics, resulting in a diffuse climatic signal. In contrast, bioclimatic spectra more directly resolve glacial–interglacial climatic gradients and show greater robustness to incomplete faunal lists and taphonomic biases. Our results demonstrate that bioclimatic spectra provide a clearer palaeoclimatic signal than habitat‐based approaches for fluvial microvertebrate assemblages. This method is therefore particularly well suited to Quaternary environmental reconstruction in lowland river systems affected by taphonomic and sedimentary filtering.</jats:p>

items.title: Bioclimatic and habitat signals in Pleistocene fluvial microvertebrate assemblages from the Middle Dnipro region, Ukraine

items.abstract: <jats:p>Of the three substantial areas of postglacial aerial exposure on the Irish Sea shelf (Liverpool Bay, Cardigan Bay and the Bristol Channel), Cardigan Bay is the largest and the one about which we know the least. This article provides the first empirical sea level data for Cardigan Bay since the 1980s. It examines the proposition that the valleys of north Cardigan Bay were subject to a long period of marine influence that is not modelled in current palaeogeographical reconstructions. Detailed lithostratigraphic investigations traced the extent of Early to Mid‐Holocene marine influence in the Dysynni valley. Multiple microfossil proxies were used to calculate sea level data points. Two sea level index points from a back‐barrier marsh indicated relative sea level rise from −5.55 to −3.13 mOD between 7790–7630 and 6399–6296 cal. a BP. Freshwater/terrestrial limiting points from 7 km inland bracketed a period of marine influence between 9889–9545 and 4783–4416 cal. a BP. Pollen recorded a transition from saltmarsh, fen and reed‐swamp environments to alder carr and then birch woodland. The results were combined with existing lithostratigraphic and biostratigraphic data to show that the overdeepened glacial valleys of north Cardigan Bay were subject to marine influence from before 12 000 cal. a BP, with different palaeogeographical histories dependent on their depths and rates of postglacial sedimentation.</jats:p>
